one_liner: Yrs, the Rust port of the Yjs CRDT, as a WebAssembly npm module: loads Yjs documents faster but edits slower than Yjs.
what_it_does: ywasm wraps the yrs Rust core (same repo) with wasm-bindgen so JavaScript can create YDoc instances and edit YText, YArray, YMap and XML types while producing the Yjs v1/v2 binary update format, so it can sync with Yjs peers and read stored Yjs documents. The API is not Yjs's: you call new Y.YDoc({}), open explicit transactions (doc.writeTransaction / beginTransaction) and pass them to each method, and free them to commit. Sibling bindings of the same core exist for C (yffi), Python (pycrdt), Ruby, .NET, Swift and Kotlin.
how_it_is_fast: Yrs implements the same YATA algorithm and block structure as Yjs (yrs README) in Rust, built with LTO, codegen-units=1, opt-level 3 and panic=abort (workspace release profile). Its measurable edge is decoding updates in compiled code and keeping blocks in wasm linear memory rather than as JS objects, which shows up as lower parseTime (20 of 21 rows) and near-zero JS heap use. The cost side is the boundary: in the benchmark harness each edit is three wasm-bindgen calls (writeTransaction, insert, free) plus an update callback that copies a Uint8Array out, against plain method calls in Yjs.
when_to_use: Loading or syncing large stored Yjs documents in JS where parse time dominates: B4x100 (10.5M-character document) parses in 1,328 ms vs 2,622 ms for Yjs, B4 in 16 vs 39 ms.
Keeping CRDT state off the JS GC heap: Yjs used 327.1 MB of JS heap after B4x100; ywasm's document lives in wasm memory (not measured by the suite, so check total RSS yourself).
Mixed-language stacks where a Rust (yrs), Python (pycrdt) or other yrs-based backend and JS clients should share one CRDT implementation and identical behaviour.
Append- or prepend-heavy bulk editing: B1.3 prepend 23 vs 119 ms, B1.8 append numbers 29 vs 148 ms, B1.10 28 vs 122 ms (ywasm 0.9.3).
when_not_to_use: Keystroke-by-keystroke editing with one transaction per edit: on the real-world LaTeX trace ywasm 0.9.3 took 28,675 ms vs 5,714 ms for Yjs (5.0x slower, about 110 vs 22 us per edit, derived from page data) and 4.6x slower on B4x100.
Bundle-size-sensitive pages: 213,833 bytes gzipped vs 20,100 for Yjs in the table, and the npm package grew from 767,016 bytes unpacked (0.9.3) to 1,226,037 (0.28.0).

Apps built on the Yjs ecosystem (y-websocket, y-webrtc, editor bindings): the repo's feature matrix lists no WebSocket or WebRTC provider for ywasm and marks its shared-type and document observers as incompatible with Yjs.
Inserting words at random positions: B1.5 449 vs 154 ms; B1.4 and B1.11 are a wash (128 vs 131 ms, 144 vs 134 ms).

integration.form: module (npm package ywasm, 0.28.0; the Rust core is the yrs crate)
integration.dependencies: yrs, wasm-bindgen, js-sys, serde-wasm-bindgen, base64_light; console_error_panic_hook on by default
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2018 with wasm-bindgen to build; consumers need a JS runtime with WebAssembly (minimum Node or browser version not documented)
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly-capable JS runtime (the suite ran Node 20.5.0; it also has Bun and browser scripts)
integration.thread_safety: One active transaction per document; ywasm's doc comment says further attempts throw an exception. Not designed for sharing across workers.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — wire-compatible with Yjs (same update format; docSize identical to Yjs in the table), but a different JS API with explicit transactions, observers that differ from Yjs's, and no Yjs provider integration

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the published table: the ywasm 0.9.3 column was produced with benchmarks/ywasm/factory.js as of commits 362d241/8203fde (2024-01-24), whose transact() did `this.txn = this.txn || this.ydoc.beginTransaction()` and then free()d and nulled the transaction in finally. A nested insertText therefore committed the outer batch after the first edit, so in B2.2-B2.4 every ywasm edit ran as its own transaction and was applied to the peer one at a time while Yjs sent one batched update per side. The update sizes show it: B2.2 177,007 vs 33,444 bytes (about 6,000 updates of 29.5 bytes, matching B1.4's 29-byte per-edit update) with identical docSize, while the single-op B2.1 matches (6,094 both). In B3 the old applyUpdate called Y.applyUpdateV2(this.ydoc, update) outside the open transaction, so 1,540 updates were integrated one by one against Yjs's single transaction. The 3-16x B2.2-B2.4 and B3 losses are not like-for-like. Commit e03faa1 (2024-02-09, 'fixed ywasm@0.17 benchmark') fixed both paths, but the README table was never re-run.

The B4 section of the suite's README says all actions replay in a single transaction, but js-lib/b4.js calls insertText/deleteText once per edit with no transact wrapper on both sides. B4 is like-for-like (per-edit transactions with an update listener for both), so the 5x B4 loss stands for 0.9.3. Every row is a single perf.now() sample with no warm-up or repetition (js-lib/utils.js benchmarkTime), and the current ywasm run.js skips B4x100.

Transactions must be released: ywasm transactions auto-commit only when free()d, and a document allows one active transaction, so a leaked transaction blocks later edits. Text indices are UTF-16 code units (YDoc sets OffsetKind::Utf16), which matches JS strings but not the byte offsets of other yrs bindings.

Open core issues: #233 'Unsound Unsafe Implementation for BlockPtr and BranchPtr' (open since 2022-12-28); #496 reports a slowdown from the RwLock added for multi-threading in single-threaded use (open; the maintainer said B4 showed no serious change); #516 is a panic on out-of-bounds range removal through yffi.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ywasm over Loro or Automerge when you must stay wire-compatible with existing Yjs peers, servers or stored documents, or share one yrs core with non-JS backends. On raw editing speed in wasm, Loro beat Yjs on the same table's real-world trace (3,089 vs 5,714 ms) while ywasm lost it 5x, and plain Yjs remains the faster choice for per-keystroke editing in JS.
verified_claims_summary: In dmonad/crdt-benchmarks (written by Kevin Jahns, who also co-maintains y-crdt and wrote Yjs), N=6000 on an Intel i5-8400 with Node 20.5.0, ywasm 0.9.3 beat Yjs 13.6.11 on parse time in 20 of 21 rows and on prepend/append microbenchmarks (up to 5.2x), but lost the real-world editing trace 28,675 vs 5,714 ms. Its large B2.2-B2.4 and B3 losses came from a benchmark adapter that ran each ywasm edit or update as its own transaction while Yjs batched, so those rows do not measure the library like-for-like; no table for current ywasm (0.28.0) exists.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-30, v0.28.0 released 2026-09-17 on npm; crates.io stops at ywasm 0.19.2), MIT, 2.2k stars; usable today, but the only published comparison is a 2024 run of ywasm 0.9.3 through a since-fixed adapter, so measure your own workload before switching from Yjs.
